h1: The 6 Best Diskless NAS Enclosures of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Diskless NAS Enclosures: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six diskless NAS and drive enclosures from Synology, UGREEN and TerraMaster, with RAID options and who each one suits.
summary: The Synology DS925+ is the best diskless NAS enclosure for buyers who want a long-term app and camera platform, with four bays, upgradeable RAM and RAID 5, SHR and RAID 10. The DS423 delivers four-bay redundancy for less, and the DS725+ is the expandable two-bay route. The DS223j suits first-timers, the UGREEN DH2300 is the budget NAS, and the TERRAMASTER D4-320 is a fast direct-attached box, not a network one.
intro: Buying a diskless NAS splits your spending into two decisions, the box and the drives, and most regrets come from making them in the wrong order. A cheap enclosure can lock you into a short list of approved drives. A direct-attached box that looks like a NAS can turn out to share nothing across the network at all. The enclosure you choose sets the rules for every disk you buy afterwards.

We reviewed six enclosures on paper and scored them on the Primea framework, weighing bay count, platform, RAID support, drive compatibility and room to expand. Price buckets keep the comparison honest. Software ecosystems and drive rules mattered as much as hardware, because both shape what the box will still do in three years.

products.name: Synology 4-Bay DiskStation DS925+ (Diskless)
products.verdict: The long-term app platform, if you accept its drive rules.
products.description:
The DS925+ is a four-bay Plus-series enclosure with upgradeable RAM, RAID 5, SHR and RAID 10 support, and access to DSM including Surveillance Station. SHR, Synology Hybrid RAID, lets you mix drive sizes and still protect your data, which is why it matters for people who buy disks over time. It sits in the $500 and up bucket.

It tops the list because it offers the most room to grow in apps and memory. That headroom is what separates it from the DS423, which keeps four bays but cannot add RAM.

Buy it for long-term photo, backup and camera workloads. The catch is the listing's compatibility warnings for non-Synology drives on 2024 and newer Plus-series units. Check the approved list before you buy disks, or you may pay more than you planned.

products.name: Synology DS423 4-Bay Diskless NAS
products.verdict: Four-bay RAID without the Plus-series price.
products.description:
The DS423 is a four-bay NAS supporting RAID 5 and SHR, with Video Surveillance Station support plus Photo Vault and secure file sharing apps, in the $200 to $500 bucket. Four bays are the sweet spot for redundancy: RAID 5 survives one drive failure while still giving you three drives of usable space.

It ranks second because it gives you the same four bays as the DS925+ for far less, trading away upgradeable memory and the Plus-series extras. Against the DS725+, it offers more capacity up front for a lower price.

Buy it for a family or small office that wants redundancy and shared photos. The caveat is app headroom: do not expect it to run heavy workloads or many services at once, because the hardware is below the Plus tier.
products.idealFor: Families and small offices wanting redundancy.

products.name: Synology DS725+ Expandable 2-Bay Diskless NAS
products.verdict: Start with two bays and add more later.
products.description:
The DS725+ is a two-bay Plus-series NAS that supports an expansion unit for extra bays, with upgradeable RAM and private cloud and small-business features. Expansion is the argument: you start with two drives and grow later without migrating to a new box.

It lands third because the DS423 gives four bays now for less, and you pay a premium here for the expansion path. In the $500 and up bucket it also carries the same drive compatibility warnings as the DS925+, which can raise the cost of future disks.

Buy it if you expect to outgrow two bays and want to stay on one platform. Skip it if two bays will be enough forever, because the money is better spent on the DS423 or even the DS223j.
products.idealFor: Buyers who plan to expand later.

products.name: Synology 2-Bay DiskStation DS223j (Diskless)
products.verdict: Simple mirrored backup on a value-series box.
products.description:
The DS223j is a two-bay value-series NAS with soldered RAM, RAID 1 mirroring and the full DSM operating system, in the $200 to $500 bucket. RAID 1 writes every file to both drives, which is the simplest protection to understand and recover from, and exactly what a first-time buyer needs.

It sits fourth because it is modest in power and its soldered RAM cannot be upgraded. It does avoid the Plus-series drive restrictions the listing flags for the pricier models, so disks are easier to source than for the DS725+.

Choose it for personal backup, shared family storage and light media use. Skip it if you plan to run many apps, because soldered memory means no upgrade path and little room for Surveillance Station.
products.skipIf: You plan to run many apps.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300 2-Bay Desktop NAS (Diskless)
products.verdict: The cheapest true NAS here, on a non-Synology platform.
products.description:
The UGREEN DH2300 is a two-bay desktop NAS supporting up to 64TB total, running UGREEN NAS OS with its own hardware compatibility list. It sits in the $100 to $200 bucket, the cheapest true NAS in this guide, and it undercuts every Synology here on price.

It ranks fifth because its software ecosystem is smaller than DSM, with fewer mature apps for cameras and photos, and it is not DSM at all. Against the DS223j, you save money and give up polish and a long-proven platform.

It suits budget buyers comfortable with a newer platform. Check the drive compatibility list before buying disks, since the DH2300 follows UGREEN's own list and not Synology's, and a drive that is not on it can cause trouble.
products.skipIf: You want a mature app store.

products.name: TERRAMASTER D4-320 4-Bay USB 3.2 Gen2 Enclosure (Diskless)
products.verdict: A fast 4-bay RAID box, but not shared on the network.
products.description:
The TERRAMASTER D4-320 is a four-bay direct-attached enclosure using USB 3.2 Gen2 Type-C at 10Gbps, with hot-swappable bays and plug and play RAID, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Direct-attached means it behaves like a very large external drive on one computer, and 10Gbps keeps that fast.

It ranks last because it is not a NAS. It connects to a single host and cannot share files across your network like the Synology and UGREEN boxes, and it has no apps. Its lowest cost per bay is the only reason it appears at all.

It is the right buy for one computer that needs bulk, fast RAID storage, such as a video editor. Skip it if several devices, phones or family members need access.
products.idealFor: One computer needing bulk RAID storage.

methodology.title: NAS or DAS
methodology.description: We separated network storage from direct-attached boxes, since they solve different problems.

whatMatters.detail: A NAS joins your network and serves files to many devices, while a DAS plugs into one computer, like a large external drive. Buyers confuse them constantly because both are called enclosures. Look for network-attached or direct-attached wording in the title, and check whether the listing mentions an operating system such as DSM. A real NAS has one.

Bay count and RAID decide how your data is protected. RAID 1 mirrors two drives and survives one failure, RAID 5 spreads parity over three or more, and SHR handles mixed drive sizes. More bays give more flexibility. Check the RAID levels in the spec bullets, because a two-bay box cannot offer RAID 5 at all. Remember that RAID is not a backup, so plan a second copy.

Drive compatibility describes which disks the enclosure officially supports. Some newer Plus-series units warn about non-Synology drives, which can raise cost or limit support. The UGREEN keeps its own list. Search the maker's compatibility list before buying drives, and confirm the model you plan to buy is on it. Skipping this step is how a cheap disk becomes an expensive problem.

RAM and expansion determine how long a NAS stays useful. Upgradeable memory and expansion units extend its life, while soldered RAM, as on the DS223j, cannot change. Look for the words upgradeable or expansion in the listing, and think about whether you will run apps like Surveillance Station that need more memory. Buy the headroom now if you can, since soldered parts stay as shipped.

The software ecosystem is the set of apps the NAS runs, such as surveillance, photo and sync tools. DSM offers a large library, while newer platforms like UGREEN NAS OS have fewer. Browse the maker's app list before choosing, because the apps you actually use matter more than the hardware inside the box. Check that the specific apps you want exist on that platform.

cards.text: Shared over the network with apps and remote access. Picks: Synology DS925+, DS423, DS725+, DS223j and UGREEN DH2300.

cards.text: Fast storage for one computer, no network sharing. Pick: TERRAMASTER D4-320.

howToChoose.note: Most buyers should choose a true NAS unless one computer is all that matters.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: RAID 1 or SHR mirroring, simple setup and a reputable software platform.

cards.text: You run cameras or many apps. The Synology DS925+ has the headroom.

cards.text: You only back up files. The Synology DS223j or UGREEN NAS DH2300 are enough.

faq.a: No, all six are diskless, so you buy the drives separately. Check the compatibility list first, especially on the DS925+ and DS725+, where Synology warns about non-Synology drives on 2024 and newer Plus-series units. Budget for the drives, since they often cost more than the box.

Buying a direct-attached box and expecting network sharing. The TERRAMASTER D4-320 connects to a single computer over USB and shares nothing, while the Synology and UGREEN units are true NAS. Read the title for the words network or direct-attached before you order.

faq.q: Is the DS925+ worth it over the DS423?
faq.a: Only if you need upgradeable RAM and heavy apps like Surveillance Station. For backup, photo storage and file sharing, the DS423 offers four bays and RAID 5 for much less money.

faq.q: How do I set up RAID?
faq.a: Install the drives, set up the operating system and choose the RAID level. A two-bay unit like the DS223j uses RAID 1 mirroring, while the DS423 offers RAID 5 or SHR across four drives.

Keep the firmware updated and watch the drive health notices. Replace a failed drive promptly in a RAID array, and let the rebuild finish before you trust the data again. Also keep a separate backup copy.

faq.q: Can the UGREEN use any drive?
faq.a: It has its own hardware compatibility list rather than Synology's, so check it before buying disks. The DH2300 supports up to 64TB total, but only drives the maker approves are safe.

finalTake: Start with what the box must do. The DS925+ is the best long-term platform but comes with Synology's drive warnings and the highest price bucket. The DS423 gives most families the redundancy they need for less, and the DS223j is a clean first NAS. Take the UGREEN only if you are comfortable with a newer platform, and buy the D4-320 only for one computer.
